list.listitem: Suspect traumatic hyphema in patients presenting with blood in the anterior chamber, often in the setting of ocular trauma or eye surgery. Perform complete examination of the eye and orbit to rule out other serious injuries. C

Small (grade 1 or <1/3 of anterior chamber) hyphemas do not require hospitalization but require daily slit lamp and intraocular pressure examinations for several days. This will require ophthalmology referral in almost all cases. C
Nonpharmacologic interventions, such as eye patching, head elevation, and bed rest show no evidence of effect for secondary hemorrhage or time to rebleed. B
The use of systemic or topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics to improve important patient outcomes for traumatic hyphema is not supported by evidence. B
While systemic antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid may reduce rebleeding, they do not improve visual acuity and may increase adverse events like nausea and vomiting. B
Most traumatic hyphemas resolve without significant sequelae. B
Adequate eye protection should be used for any activity with risk for eye injury (eg, occupational, racquet sports, etc.). C

background.definition: Hyphema is hemorrhage into the anterior chamber of the eye. It is almost always the result of trauma. Sports and occupational injuries are the most common causes. The severity of hyphema is graded according to what percentage of the anterior chamber is filled with blood.

list.listitem: 12 per 100,000 per year.
Male to female incidence 4:1 (due to higher risk of trauma and occupational exposure).
Thirty percent to 40% percent are the result of athletics; racquet sports, softball, and baseball have the highest risk.
Up to 80% of traumatic hyphemas have other associated eye injuries.
Trauma (the vast majority).
Neovascularization with hemorrhage (diabetic).
Tumor (retinoblastoma).
Other vascular abnormalities (xanthogranuloma).
Hemophilias, anticoagulants.
Blood accumulates in the anterior chamber after trauma.
Secondary complications can include glaucoma, optic atrophy, staining of the cornea, and reduced vision.
Most hyphemas are grade 1 (less than one-third of the anterior chamber filled with blood) and resolve spontaneously within 5 days.

Adequate eye protection should be used for any activity with risk for eye injury (eg, occupational, racquet sports, etc.). While the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) provides standards for prescription glasses and industrial safety eyewear, there remains signicant research gaps on the most optimal lens, frame, and product material for eye protection.C
Children with sickle cell trait who sustain traumatic hyphemas are at a higher risk for elevated intraocular pressure, secondary hemorrhage, and permanent visual deficits after blunt trauma.

Patients with a history of sickle cell or sickle cell trait have a greater risk of glaucoma, optic atrophy, and vision loss following traumatic hyphema; in regions where newborn sickle cell screening is not routine, consider screening of high-risk individuals.
Initial diagnosis is made by visualizing blood in the anterior chamber. C
Complete examination of the eye and orbit are required to determine whether other serious injuries are present. C
Serial examinations are required to observe for rebleeding and increased intraocular pressure. C
Hyphema typically occurs after trauma from a projectile to the eye.
Spontaneous hyphemas can occur rarely. These should prompt evaluation for bleeding disorders, such as hemophilia or thrombocytopenia.
Physical examination should focus on grading the hyphema (see ) and carefully searching for evidence of other associated injuries.
Associated injuries may include bony injury to the orbit or injury to the globe, lens, or retina.
Slit lamp examination with applanation tonometry is recommended for all patients.
Other evaluations as required include direct or indirect fundoscopy and b-mode ultrasound.
Take plain radiographs of the orbit for fracture or suspected foreign body.
Order CT of the orbit if bony injury is suspected (more sensitive than plain films).
Diagnosis is made by examination of the anterior chamber of the eye.
Thorough investigation for other injuries (to the globe, vitreous, orbit) is necessary.
Daily slit lamp examinations are required to follow the hyphema and test for secondary acute glaucoma.
See algorithm in .
Nonpharmacologic interventions, such as eye patching, head elevation, and bed rest show no evidence of effect for secondary hemorrhage or time to rebleed. B
The use of systemic or topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics to improve important patient outcomes for traumatic hyphema is not supported by evidence. B
While systemic antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid may reduce rebleeding, they do not improve visual acuity and may increase adverse events like nausea and vomiting. B
Consider pain medications and antiemetics as needed. C
Consider using medications to reduce intraocular pressure as needed based on serial pressure measurements. C
Cycloplegics (topical) are commonly used to reduce pain (particularly if there is associated iritis). Topical analgesia (proparacaine or tetracaine) may give temporary relief.
Give intraocular pressure-lowering medications such as topical beta blockers if there is evidence of elevated intraocular pressure.

Give pain medication and antiemetics as needed. While experts recommend avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin, a small RCT found no evidence that use of aspirin increases rebleeding in patients with traumatic hyphema.

Tranexamic acid and fibrinolytics (eg, aminocaproic acid) may reduce rebleeding rates but have not been shown to improve final visual acuity. Use of systemic aminocaproic acid can slow resolution of hyphema and lead to increased nausea and vomiting. Actual use of these therapies varies widely in practice.
Topical tranexamic acid was found to reduce the time to layered blood resolution and decrease the frequency of rebleeding compared to systemic cortiocsteroids.

A Cochrane review identified 23 randomized and seven quasi-randomized studies with a total of 2969 participants. Interventions included antifibrinolytic agents (systemic and topical aminocaproic acid, tranexamic acid, and aminomethylbenzoic acid), corticosteroids (systemic and topical), cycloplegics, miotics, aspirin, conjugated estrogens, traditional Chinese medicine, monocular versus bilateral patching, elevation of the head, and bed rest. None were found to be effective in improving visual acuity.
Any specific clotting abnormalities (eg, hemophilia, warfarin use, thrombocytopenia) should be addressed if possible.
Remove blood from the anterior chamber if there are signs of corneal staining or excess intraocular pressures.
The likelihood of need for surgical therapy is closely correlated with the grade of the hyphema.
Reading should be limited to reduce visual accomodation so as not to further stress injured blood vessels.
Eye shield is preferred over occlusive patch with gauze and antibacterial ointment.
Patients must be followed in a setting in which they can have appropriate serial examinations. This will require referral to ophthalmology for almost all cases.
Patients with minor (grade 1) hyphemas may be managed as outpatients.
Hospitalization may be considered for children if there is concern about ability to follow activity restrictions.
Most traumatic hyphemas resolve without significant sequelae. B
Prognosis for visual outcome may be affected by the grade of the hyphema and other associated injuries. C
Rebleeding and significantly increased intraocular pressure may predict worse prognosis. C
The incidence of synechiae, which can be associated with angle closure and pupillary block glaucoma, is higher in patients when hyphema persits beyond eight days. C

Sequelae such as anisocoria (from torn iris sphincter muscles) and corneal blood staining (golden discoloration of the cornea related to diffusion of red blood cell breakdown products into the corenal stroma) may result in decreased visual acuity. C
Long-term endothelial loss and increased lenticular density can occur even in uncomplicated traumatic hyphema. B
Weigh the risks and benefits of aminocaproic acid for pregnant patients in the absence of human or animal data from clinical trials.
Children may have a higher incidence of rebleeding, although expectant management is not different.
Children with sickle cell disease and hemophilia are at increased risk of complications.
